summary:
## The Case Against Docker

- **Monetization Issues**: Docker's business model for commercial use can be problematic, involving:
    - **Docker Hub Rate Limits**: Frequent image pulls can be throttled unless you pay for a token.
    - **Docker Desktop Licensing**: Commercial use of Docker Desktop on Mac and Windows requires a paid subscription for larger companies, which can lead to legal complications.
- **OCI Standard**: Popular Kubernetes services often use other OCI-compliant runtimes like **containerd**, not Docker Engine itself, demonstrating that Docker is not the only option.

## Introducing Podman: The Open-Source Alternative

Podman is a powerful alternative to Docker that is:
- **Free & Open Source**: No licensing fees for commercial or personal use.
- **Daemonless & Rootless**: Enhances security by not requiring a central, privileged daemon running as root.
- **A Drop-in Replacement**: The CLI is designed to be an alias for the Docker CLI, making the transition seamless (`alias docker=podman`).

> [!NOTE]
> On macOS or Windows, you must first create and start a Linux VM for Podman to use. This is done with `podman machine init` and `podman machine start`.

## The Power of Pods

Podman natively supports **pods**, a concept borrowed from Kubernetes, which are groups of co-located containers that share resources.
- **Creation**: Use `podman pod create <name>` to start a new pod.
- **`infra` Container**: Every pod runs a tiny `infra` container to manage the shared network namespace.
- **Communication**: Containers within the same pod can communicate with each other directly using `localhost`.

## From Podman to Kubernetes

Podman provides a killer feature for bridging local development with Kubernetes deployment.
- **`podman generate kube <pod_name>`**: Automatically generates a Kubernetes-compatible YAML manifest from a running Podman pod.
- **`podman play kube <file.yaml>`**: Deploys a Kubernetes YAML file locally using Podman, allowing you to test configurations before moving to a cluster.

> [!TIP]
> This workflow allows you to build and test a multi-container application locally as a pod and then effortlessly generate the configuration needed to deploy it to any Kubernetes cluster.

## Podman Desktop: A Powerful UI

Podman Desktop is a graphical interface for managing your entire container ecosystem.

**Key Features**:
- **Unified Management**: View and manage containers, pods, images, and volumes from both Podman and Docker.
- **Container Interaction**: Access live log streams, inspect configurations, and open a terminal directly inside a running container.
- **Kubernetes Dashboard**: A built-in dashboard that can connect to your local Minikube cluster or any configured remote Kubernetes cluster, providing a full-featured UI for cluster management.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The integrated Kubernetes dashboard in Podman Desktop is an incredibly powerful tool, offering visibility into nodes, services, configs, and more, all from one place.
transcription:
## The Problem with Docker's Ubiquity

You know how people say 'Google it' to describe any online search? Where I'm from, we use 'Jeep' to describe any 4x4 vehicle. The same goes for Zoom when describing video conferencing. This is exactly what happens with Docker.

Think about it, you use `docker build`, `docker tag`, `docker create`, `docker run`. I've been doing the same for over 10 years now as a DevOps engineer and then as a cloud architect. But it's 2024 and there are different container runtimes now. Look at the most popular Kubernetes services, for example. They're not actually running Docker; the backend runtime is something else, like containerD. These alternatives follow the OCI, which is the Open Container Initiative, which was created to standardize container specifications so you're not locked into one solution.

## Why You Might Be Breaking the Law Using Docker

But why am I even telling you this? Well Docker, the company, wasn't making enough money. About two years ago, they decided to monetize their CLI usage. For instance, when you use `docker push` or `docker pull` without specifying a registry, the Docker CLI automatically uses Docker Hub, their managed registry, but Docker Hub isn't the only option. Suddenly, companies using Docker Hub for pushing and pulling images throughout the day started hitting rate limits. Their work ground to a halt unless they paid Docker for a token.

Sure, you can solve this by switching registries. Use AWS ECR, Google GCR, GitHub, Quay, and a bunch of others. But here's the real issue: just like Docker Hub, you now have to pay to use Docker on your own machine. If you're on a Mac running Docker Desktop, for example, and you're running `docker build` or `docker run`, `docker push`, etc. for commercial purposes, you might be breaking the law. And if you don't want to end up floating in the middle of the ocean locked in a shipping container—because that's what they do with container criminals, right?—you might want to reconsider your next move.

## Podman: The Open-Source Docker Alternative

If your company isn't paying for Docker licenses, consider Podman. It's open source, it does everything Docker does, so basically a drop-in replacement with a simpler CLI that's free for both commercial and personal use. It's faster, it's safer, it's daemonless, and we'll get to all of that. And here's how it works.

Podman, as the landing page suggests, is the best free and open-source container tool system, and it is downloadable for any major platform. To make my life easier, I just went with Brew, but any method works. With Podman ready to go, we can start using its man pages for all options and necessary explanations, which are also available in its brief version through the help flag. Okay, let's get cracking.

## Getting Started with Podman Commands

The first thing you want to do if you're not running on Linux is creating a Podman machine. Containers run natively on Linux platforms, and in my case, Mac OS requires an intermediary. When it's initiated, you can start it, and there we are. `podman machine ls` will provide the list of running machines. And as a nusual hipster, I have to show off and detach columns to have a pretty table view of machine data that I can select the name from specifically. More on nusual and how it improved my workflow in the video above.

I've mentioned that Podman is first and foremost a drop-in replacement for Docker, and it is. We can search for images with `podman search`. Here's a list of available Redis images, which again I'll pretty-print with my shell to make them more readable. Podman comes with a very useful filter flag, allowing us to grab only official images, which is what you're looking for nine out of 10 times, unless you're a fan of running rogue applications built in the wild by strangers. Let's run a container. Much like Docker, we provide a port mapping, an image, and all other flags that translate directly. You can basically alias Docker to Podman and for the most part, you're not going to see the difference. So Engine X is running. Let's grab a browser and prove that there's no black magic here. And there we are, welcome to Engine X.

## Managing Containers & The Daemonless Advantage

Like `docker ps`, `podman ps` shows running containers. Like Docker, Podman uses `-d` to run detached containers in the background. Here's Engine X again, and here's the container listed by Podman with all the usuals as Docker outputs: an ID, image, command, status, ports, and those random names, which if you're ever wondering how they make out these great names, it's not AI, it's just a long, long dictionary of names combined together into hilarious results. Before we dive in, let me tell you about today's sponsor...

## Sponsor: Twingate

Twingate, the smart way to secure your remote access. You know how traditional VPNs are like having a single fortress gate? Once someone's in, they can wander anywhere. Well, Twingate flips this model on its head with zero-trust security. Think of it as a modern city where every district requires its own access path—much safer, right?

But here's what's really cool, especially for you developers out there: Twingate now seamlessly integrates with Kubernetes. So instead of bouncing between engineering and IT teams, you can configure secure access right in your YAML files. It's all part of the regular engineering flow, no context switching needed. Setup takes minutes, not days, and works across all of your devices. Plus, you get enterprise-grade security without the enterprise-grade headaches. Whether you're managing a remote team or running complex Kubernetes deployments, Twingate handles the security heavy lifting, and you can focus on what really matters: building great software. Ready to level up your remote access security? Head over to twingate.com for a free trial and see why thousands of teams trust Twingate with their secure access needs.

## Working with Podman

So our stoic Woo is ready to be killed. We can use the name or ID. Let's go with the ID and it's gone. Now here's a trick for you container users: both Docker and Podman support `ps -q` resulting in a quiet list of IDs. So you can do it with any number of containers, but especially when you have one of them, you can run `podman kill` and then, wrapped in a subshell command, grab the ID of the container you have using `podman ps -q`. If there's more than one, you can pick the last one using `--last 1`.

Moving on, like Docker, Podman has the `top` subcommand with running processes, which if we tidy up a little, shows the current container, its running processes, and how much they're consuming. Now here's an important differentiator of Podman: while Docker needs its Docker socket to run, which is also running as root, Podman is daemonless and rootless. If you grab processes mentioning Podman, there are none, but Docker needs a bunch of them. Let's grab the user off of the `ls` output for Docker socket to prove the point. So these are critical but rather basic differences you're not going to mind daily. What is actually the best selling point for Podman is actually in its name: pods.

## Understanding Podman Pods

If you're thinking about Kubernetes, you're not alone. Podman, unlike Docker, lets you gather multiple containers in pods and have them run together. To access them through the CLI, Podman comes with `podman pod`, which we can then run `ps` on to grab a list of running pods. Let's create one and name it `webapp`. Sorry for the lack of creativity here. Now you may be surprised, this is already running even before we even told it to run anything. Every pod runs an internal infra container. An infra container is a lightweight container used to coordinate the shared kernel namespace of a pod, which is just fancy words saying it's an admin layer to help make sure everything is in order. 

Let's pour some stuff into the new pod. We can run `-d` for detached, point the command to the pod, name the container redis, and run, well, Redis. We've got too much information here to view the running containers, so let's grab the not-so-beautifully parsed number under the column named '#' showing us two of them. We can also run `podman inspect` to see the same JSON including both hash and state.

## Inter-Container Communication within a Pod

Okay, let's test it. The nice thing about containers in a pod is that they don't have to have anything special to communicate with each other and can basically ping each other using localhost. Let's run a third container in the pod. Using `--rm`, we'll make sure it's deleted as soon as it's exited, and use `redis-cli` with localhost as the target host to send a Redis command. And let's write the key named `mykey` which will hold `hello from redis`. We've got a good result from the server, which is nice. So let's run another verification to read the key. Same idea, just `get mykey` and there's our string, `hello from redis`. Cool.

So far, nothing fancy, but it works. If you want to run a container and connect to it within the pod, same as with Docker, we can exec into it, connecting to a shell. Since Alpine doesn't come with bash, we'll just use the old `sh`. Install `redis` quickly and send a `redis-ping` to localhost that comes back with `PONG`. All working as expected. By the way, here's something cool by Redis: if we try to `curl` localhost with the Redis port, and just to see what happens in a split, let's pop the Redis logs on screen... I get an empty reply from the server, but the logs below are actually showing Redis has detected my attempt as a security attack, so it blocks non-standard Redis communication altogether. I didn't know that is even possible before.

## The Killer Feature: Generating Kubernetes Manifests

Right, so far so good. But if you're using or planning to use Kubernetes, the next feature is a real killer. Let's say that we want to create a separate new application with Engine X and PostgreSQL as an example. We'll run Engine X and call it `web`, and then run PostgreSQL and call it `db`. Check this out: we can now run `podman generate kube web db` and I'll send it to a YAML file so we can easily review the output. Now look at that, a Kubernetes YAML ready to go using my two containers in a pod with volume mounts and everything you need to throw it in a cluster. But before we'll do that, we have a YAML, right? What if we want to recreate it? Check this: `podman play kube` and a YAML lets you run the Kubernetes YAML files describing your pods locally. With our deployment running, `podman ps` reveals Engine X and PostgreSQL just started, and running `podman pod ps` shows it as a running pod.

Are you thinking what I'm thinking? There's no way this actually runs in a cluster. So let's do exactly that. First off, a small adjustment. Our deployment holds volumes and I'd have to create them in Kubernetes with this name, so let me elegantly shorten the name and send the volume mount to basically nowhere using `emptyDir`. If these kind of things interest you and you want to dive deeper, check this out. If all that Kubernetes talk is actually getting you curious and you'd like to jump in, I have a getting started self-paced digital workshop just for you. It'll get you from absolute novice to running your own cluster with a running web application, a database, and everything you need to get yourself familiar with the basics and create some working experience. Check the description for more.

## Deploying Podman Manifests to a Kubernetes Cluster

With the YAML ready, let's make sure Minikube is on. Minikube is also covered thoroughly in my workshop if that's of interest. Okay, the cluster is empty. Let's apply the pod, and voila, it's created. Now, there's an error due to PostgreSQL naturally not being able to find the volume, but nevertheless, the code is applied and accepted by the cluster. That is a big win. We can even query some logs with `kubectl` to see Engine X starting its workers in the background.

## A Tour of Podman Desktop UI

Last but very much not least, Podman comes with Podman Desktop, a UI that does a lot. When you first launch it, it offers onboarding with some extremely useful extensions, like being able to use `podman-compose` like `docker-compose` with existing setups out of the box, as well as `kubectl` for other options from within the UI. With that out of the way, here's the UI showing Podman and Docker running. We'll kill Docker for a minute to show the indication turning off. Under the containers tab, we get all of the containers in the system, whether active or exited. Choosing a running container will present some data, a live feed of logs, we can inspect the config from the UI and get a Kubernetes manifest ready for deployment. But beyond all that, there's a terminal shell attached to the container which we can use directly to debug my container immediately. That's some good stuff right there. 

Here's our webapp pod from earlier, showing multiple containers running under the same roof. We can also see images downloaded, volumes in the system, and get this: a Kubernetes dashboard. What? This is worth having even if you skip everything I've said so far. Let's get Docker back on so we can have our local Minikube back in operation. And with Minikube on, here's everything in a UI: the Minikube nodes, services, YAML, config maps, even an option to configure port forwarding. Now, while this is currently pointing at my local Minikube, I can change it to any other cluster I have configured and explore it remotely using Podman Desktop.

## Conclusion and Next Steps

So you've got yourself an open-source alternative to Docker and you're almost ready to take on Kubernetes. But a container manager is just the start. Here's a video with extremely useful tools I incorporated into my own workflow over the past decade. I'm sure you'll be surprised. Thank you for watching and I'll see you on the next one.
